title: From waste collection to value recovery: why each photograph was chosen
overview: The carousel follows the material along its journey in four different realistic scenes: packaging leaking out of the system, a return handover, how well it is collected and handled, and what processing turns it into. Each photograph was generated for that slide's exact message and checked by eye before use.
rules: One shared look: documentary editorial photography, soft natural daylight, 35mm eye-level perspective, shallow depth of field, Indian urban, retail and industrial settings, plain unbranded packaging, nothing legible in the image.
A light, consistent colour grade was applied to all four so they read as one series (slightly muted, true greens). Slide 2 was cooled and slide 3's strongly saturated crates were toned down.
Four different compositions, so no two slides repeat a layout or subject: full-bleed street scene on top (1), portrait handover (2), wide sorting table (3), close-up macro (4).
All text sits on white outside the photographs, so nothing competes with the images.
weak_spots: Slide 2 is a generic, plain return handover. It deliberately avoids a branded kiosk or machine, so it does not imply one specific scheme design; the cost is that it can read as an ordinary shop counter without the headline.

Photographs are AI-generated. They were checked for warped hands, objects and unreadable gibberish, but a final human look before publishing is sensible, especially at full size on slide 2 (hands) and slide 3 (wrappers).
The images illustrate stages; they do not show that any particular packaging is recycled. Collection (2), sorting and handling (3) and processing (4) are kept visually separate on purpose.

slides.title: Slide 1 – Value is at risk after consumption
slides.says: Packaging can retain value, but littering, improper disposal and gaps in collection stop it reaching recovery channels. The fix is a more organised collection system and a clear pathway to material recovery.
shows: A low, kerb-level view of an ordinary city street early in the morning: a handful of empty bottles and cans resting against the kerb beside a storm drain grating.
The street recedes into soft focus with passers-by and parked scooters: this is everyday leakage, not a dump.
The litter sits lower-left; the logo plate and heading sit on white around it.

slides.title: Slide 2 – A Deposit Refund Scheme creates a structured return pathway
slides.says: A DRS uses a nominal refundable deposit to encourage the return of eligible empty packaging, channelling it into organised collection systems where it can move towards recycling.
shows: A customer hands empty bottles across a plain counter to an attendant: the act of returning.
Behind the counter, stacked crates of collected empties: organised collection rather than loose packaging.
The warm shop interior contrasts with the cooler street of slide 1: from loose to handed in.
icons: Hands in the foreground
The return is a deliberate, repeatable action.
Crates of empties
Collected packaging held in an organised way.
No machine, no signage
Keeps the scene generic and avoids implying one scheme design.
Deposit
Carried by the copy; the image only shows the return handover.

slides.title: Slide 3 – Collection quality decides how much value is recovered
slides.says: How packaging is collected and handled affects its suitability for recycling. Contamination and poor handling reduce material quality and limit the value that can ultimately be recovered.
shows: Gloved hands sort bottles at a table between two crates, seen from the front and slightly above.
Left crate: clean, empty, dry bottles. Right crate: bottles with visible residue and food-soiled wrappers.
Same table, same worker: the only difference is how the material was collected and handled.
icons: Clean crate (left)
Material that stays suitable for recycling.
Soiled crate (right)
Contamination and poor handling that reduce quality.
Worker's hands
Handling and sorting: the human step that shapes quality.
Modest contrast
Obvious at a glance but not exaggerated.

slides.title: Slide 4 – Every stage keeps material value in circulation
slides.says: A better pathway keeps material value in circulation. DRS strengthens the return and collection of eligible packaging; sorting, processing and recycling turn it into a usable resource. The goal is for the value to find its way back into the economy.
shows: A gloved hand holds a scoop of clean shredded PET flakes inside a recycling plant, flakes falling into a bin below.
The washing and processing line stands soft in the background: this is processing, clearly after collection and sorting.
The flakes are the 'usable resource' of the copy: material that has kept its value.
